summary: Defines terms used in work on IP mobility. It came out of the Seamoby working group but was written to be useful for any IETF group dealing with mobility. It is informational.

eli5.summary: When people talk about devices moving around the network, they need to mean the same thing by the same words. This is the word list.

questions: what is the difference between macro and micro mobility
what is a handover in ip mobility
subtitle: A shared dictionary of terms for IP mobility: access networks, handovers, paging, ad-hoc networks and mobility security.

tldr.problem: People working on IP mobility came from different engineering backgrounds and used the same words for different things, which made discussion and specification work hard.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3753 collects agreed definitions in groups: general terms, access network and mobile network components, handover types, mobile node states and paging, mobile ad-hoc networking, and security.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational glossary, not a protocol. It started in the Seamoby Working Group and was written so other IETF groups working on mobility could reuse it.

today: RFC 3753 is an Informational document, published in June 2004, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. It is a vocabulary reference, not a protocol specification.

sections.title: Why a Mobility Vocabulary
sections.content:
RFC 3753 defines terminology for documents and discussions in the Seamoby Working Group, and it hopes other mobility working groups will adopt it too. It is a first step in harmonizing terms across people with many different engineering backgrounds, and it does not claim to assert new terminology.

Some terms are not strictly about IP. The RFC points out that an Access Point and a base station are the same component from the point of view of IP, while an Access Router means something very different. The document also hopes the terms are adequate for mobile ad-hoc networks.
sections.eli5: Different groups called the same thing by different names. This document picks one name for each thing so everyone can talk to each other.

sections.title: General Terms and Mobile Addressing
sections.content:
The general terms cover link and radio basics (bandwidth, channel, beacon, neighbor, next hop, payload) and routing basics (distance vector, link state, flooding, loop-free, routing table, source route).

The mobility-specific ones describe how a moving node stays reachable. A Home Address is the permanent address of a mobile node on its home link. A Care-of-Address is the address it uses while visiting a foreign link. The Home Agent is a router on the home link that intercepts packets for the home address, encapsulates them and tunnels them to the registered care-of address. A Binding Update is the message that tells others the node's current binding, in particular its care-of address.

A routing proxy is a node that routes packets by overlays, such as tunneling. The Home Agent and Foreign Agent are the examples given.
sections.eli5: Your home address is like your permanent house. When you stay at a hotel, your mail is sent to the hotel address, and a helper at home forwards it there.

sections.title: Access Networks and Mobile Networks
sections.content:
An Access Network (AN) is an IP network made of nodes near the edge that provide mobility support. The RFC names three kinds of component: Access Routers (AR), which handle the last hop to the mobile node, usually over a wireless link; Access Network Gateways (ANG), which form the boundary on the fixed network side; and optional internal Access Network Routers (ANR). An AR and an ANG may be the same physical node.

An Access Point (AP) is a layer 2 device that offers the wireless link, and the area it covers is a Radio Cell. During a move the AR currently serving the node is the Serving Access Router, the one it leaves is the Previous Access Router (PAR) and the one it joins is the New Access Router (NAR).

A Mobile Node is an IP node that can change its point of attachment. It is either a Mobile Host (no forwarding) or a Mobile Router (forwarding). A whole mobile network can move as a unit behind a Mobile Router, which has ingress interfaces inside the network and egress interfaces toward the Internet. The RFC notes that this reference architecture is not well suited to mobile ad-hoc networks.
sections.eli5: Think of the network edge as a set of Wi-Fi stations. The one you are connected to now is your serving station, and the one you walk toward is the new station.

sections.title: Handover Terminology
sections.content:
A handover (also called handoff) is the process by which an active mobile node changes its point of attachment, or when such a change is attempted. The RFC sorts handovers by scope: a Layer 2 handover stays under the same AR, an Intra-AN handover changes ARs inside one AN, and an Inter-AN handover moves to a new AN and needs macro mobility and a new IP access address. It also separates horizontal handovers (same type of access point) from vertical ones (different types, such as UMTS to WLAN), and admits the difference can be vague.

Handover control is classified along five largely independent axes: mobile-initiated or network-initiated, mobile-controlled or network-controlled, mobile-assisted, network-assisted or unassisted, push or pull, and planned or unplanned. In a make-before-break handover the new connection is made before the old one ends; in break-before-make it is not.

Performance terms include handover latency (the gap between the last packet via the PAR and the first via the NAR), smooth handover (minimize packet loss), fast handover (minimize latency) and seamless handover (no change in service capability, security or quality).
sections.eli5: Switching from one Wi-Fi station to another is a handover. You can connect to the new one before letting go of the old one, or let go first and risk a short gap.

sections.title: States, Paging, Context and Mobility Types
sections.content:
A mobile node is always in one of three states. In the Active state the network knows its Serving Access Router and it can send and receive IP packets. In the Dormant state (also called Idle) it listens less, the network knows only its paging area, and the network must page it to deliver packets. In the Inactive state it is not listening at all, for example powered off or out of range. Paging is the procedure that moves a Dormant node to Active, and location updating is how the node tells the network it entered a new paging area.

Other terms in this part cover context transfer (moving the state of a routing-related service, such as header compression, to a new router) and candidate access router discovery (Candidate AR and Target AR). Mobility types are split into host and network mobility, and into macro mobility (over a large area, between IP domains, where Mobile IP applies) and micro mobility (within an access network).
sections.eli5: A phone can be awake, napping or off. When it naps, the network only knows roughly which neighborhood it is in, and has to call out to wake it when something arrives.

sections.title: Ad-Hoc and Security Terms
sections.content:
The ad-hoc networking terms include cluster, cluster head, convergence and convergence time, laydown, pathloss matrix and scenario, which the RFC defines as the tuple of laydown, pathloss matrix, mobility factor and traffic.

The security terms are a mobility-related subset: authorization-enabling extension, mobility security association (a collection of security contexts between a pair of nodes), registration key, security context and Security Parameter Index (SPI). The RFC's own security section says that the document presents only terminology and has no security issues.
sections.eli5: The last part lists words for groups of devices that form a network on the fly, and for the secret handshakes that keep moving devices safe.

columns: Can send or receive IP packets

cells: Only the paging area; paging needed
Not necessarily an IP access address
